detail:
The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) reports on a long-term study of childhood insomnia symptoms that followed 502 children for 15 years, from around age 9 through adolescence into young adulthood. The study, funded in part by NHLBI and published in the journal Pediatrics, tracked moderate-to-severe difficulties initiating or maintaining sleep and how those symptoms changed over time, and NHLBI describes it as the first long-term cohort study to describe the developmental course of childhood insomnia symptoms into young adulthood.

The researchers found that 43% of children with insomnia symptoms continued to have them through adolescence into adulthood. About 27% experienced remission of their symptoms by adolescence, while close to 19% had a waxing and waning pattern of insomnia into adulthood. NHLBI presents the findings as evidence that the persistence of insomnia symptoms is greater than previously believed, and notes that sleep disorders such as insomnia are linked to poorer cardiovascular and mental health.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about insomnia research.
sourceName: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute
summary: An NHLBI-funded 15-year study of 502 children found that 43% of those with insomnia symptoms continued to have them into adulthood, a persistence rate researchers describe as greater than previously believed.
takeaways: the study followed 502 children over 15 years

about 27% saw their symptoms remit by adolescence
title: Insomnia: childhood symptoms often persist into adulthood, a long-term study finds
